newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss block Mobutu assets but bankers sceptical.
newsitem.headline: Swiss block Mobutu assets but bankers sceptical.

text.p: Hours after Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko was officially ousted from power, the Swiss federal government on Saturday blocked all assets that he and his family may have in Switzerland.

The decree by the Swiss Federal Council (cabinet), announced in a joint statement by the Foreign and Finance Ministries, said anyone in Switzerland handling wealth belonging to Mobutu or his family was obliged to notify the Finance Ministry immediately.
The public prosecutor of the rebel-held Zairean city of Lubumbashi asked Switzerland on Tuesday to freeze all assets Mobutu may have in the country.

In a first step, federal police and judicial authorities on Friday ordered a freeze on Mobutu's sprawling villa in Savigny, above Lausanne, valued at $5.5 million. He spent three months in the city last year after an operation for prostate cancer.
Swiss media have speculated that Mobutu, who left Kinshasa on Friday after 32 years at the helm of impoverished Zaire, may have some $4 billion stashed in this neutral Alpine haven.
But bankers in Switzerland are sceptical that Mobutu had significant financial holdings in the country after an initial informal survey of banks last month turned up no solid leads.
And legal experts, noting that funds held in Switzerland by the late Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, frozen by Berne after he was toppled in 1986, are still tied up in complex legal wrangling.
Rebels marched into Kinshasa virtually unopposed on Saturday and their leader Laurent Kabila proclaimed himself head of state, crowning seven months of civil war with victory.
Mobutu himself is expected to arrive with his family in the Moroccan capital Rabat later on Saturday, Moroccan officials said.
The Swiss order, based on article 102 of the Constitution, followed the "departure" of Mobutu, "who henceforth no longer carries out the function of President of Zaire", it said.
"The Federal Council today adopted a decree blocking the assets of the Mobutu family in Switzerland, as a provisional measure," said the joint ministry statement issued in Berne.

"Under the terms of the decree, the blocking of the assets of Mr Mobutu and the members of his family takes effect immediately and concerns wealth in Switzerland or that administered from Switzerland. Assets must not leave the country," it added.
Violating the decree was a punishable offence, it noted.

Mathias Krafft, a senior Foreign Ministry official, said it would take some time for reports to come in from bankers and asset managers on any Mobutu wealth in Switzerland under the reporting requirement in the cabinet order.
"We should have an overview in one or two weeks," he told Reuters.

In an interview with French-language Swiss Television, Krafft said of the decree: "It means that anyone handling funds belonging to the Mobutu family may not transfer them and anyone holding such funds must announce them to the Finance Ministry."
Asked whether this implied there were Mobutu funds in Swiss financial institutions, Krafft replied: "We don't know."
The order to freeze Mobutu and family assets could stay in effect for a maximum of one year, according to Krafft.
"We want to give the new authorities in Kinshasa time to provide more details," he said.

When ordering that Mobutu's 30-room villa at Savigny not be transferred, Swiss authorities said on Friday that the Lubumbashi prosecutor had not provided enough details about Mobutu's other alleged assets.
Swiss Television, in a commentary by journalist Andre Crettenand, head of its national news department, said:
"The Federal Banking Commission has already done some research and for the moment has not found much. One could therefore be fairly sceptical about what might be found.

"This was a decision obviously taken under the pressure of current events," he added. "Let us not forget that Switzerland is caught up in a storm over Nazi gold -- an affair in which Switzerland was reproached for letting its economic interests take precedence over morals.
The commentator concluded: "Switzerland would like to turn the tide."
Krafft, asked whether Mobutu might return to Switzerland to live out his last days, replied: "We have no indications that Mobutu wants to come to Switzerland.
